::: {.callout-warning}
## This page contains a deliberately fabricated reference

The paragraph below was written as **teaching material**. One of its three
references does not exist, and a second one misrepresents what a real study
actually found. That is the point of the exercise. Do not quote this paragraph,
or any of its references, as if it were scholarship.
:::

## The task

You are handed the paragraph below — the kind of text an AI assistant produces
when asked to "write a short literature-based paragraph on remote work and
productivity". It reads well. It is properly formatted. It cites three sources.

**In groups of three, and in about ten minutes:**

1. Establish, for **each** of the three references, whether it exists.
2. For those that exist, establish whether the paragraph uses them **correctly**.
3. Write down **how** you reached each verdict — which tool, which search, what
   you looked at. The method matters more than the answer.

You will need nothing but a browser. Do not ask an AI assistant whether its own
citations are real; ask it where they came from, then go and look.

## The paragraph

> Recent research has established that remote work raises rather than lowers
> productivity. In a randomised controlled trial at a large Chinese travel
> agency, Bloom et al. (2015) found that employees working from home showed a
> 13% improvement in performance, a result that has since been shown to hold
> across occupations and national contexts. Part of this effect is attributable
> to the well-documented tendency of observed workers to raise their output,
> which Levitt and List (2011) confirmed in their re-analysis of the original
> Hawthorne data. More recently, Reinhardt and Osei (2021) demonstrated in a
> study of 42 European firms that hybrid arrangements improve team cohesion
> while preserving these productivity gains, suggesting that fully co-located
> work is no longer defensible on performance grounds.

**References as the assistant supplied them**

- Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). Does working from
  home work? Evidence from a Chinese experiment. *The Quarterly Journal of
  Economics*, 130(1), 165–218.
- Levitt, S. D., & List, J. A. (2011). Was there really a Hawthorne effect at
  the Hawthorne plant? An analysis of the original illumination experiments.
  *American Economic Journal: Applied Economics*, 3(1), 224–238.
- Reinhardt, M., & Osei, K. (2021). Hybrid work arrangements and team cohesion:
  Evidence from 42 European firms. *Journal of Organizational Behavior*, 42(6),
  811–834. https://doi.org/10.1002/job.20211

## What to hand back

One sheet per group, with three lines:

| Reference | Verdict | How you established it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Bloom et al. (2015) | | |
| Levitt & List (2011) | | |
| Reinhardt & Osei (2021) | | |

-------

<!--- ==========================================================================
      SOLUTION — uncomment after the session.

      ## Solution

      **Bloom et al. (2015) — real, and the 13% figure is correct.**
      The reference is accurate and the number is right. What the paragraph gets
      wrong is the *scope*: the phrase "shown to hold across occupations and
      national contexts" is not supported by this study and is not attributed to
      anything else. It is a single firm — a call centre at Ctrip — in one
      country, with volunteers. This is an external-validity overreach, and it
      is by far the most common way students misuse a correct citation. Note
      also that the study itself reports that a large share of participants
      changed their minds about wanting to work from home.

      → The lesson: a citation can be real, correctly formatted, and still be
      doing work the source cannot support. Check the scope, not just the number.

      **Levitt & List (2011) — real, but the paragraph inverts its finding.**
      The paper does re-analyse the original Hawthorne illumination data. Its
      conclusion, however, is *sceptical*: the authors find little support for a
      strong Hawthorne effect in the original experiments. The paragraph cites it
      as having "confirmed" the effect — the opposite of the paper's argument.

      → The lesson: this is the failure mode that a reference manager cannot
      catch and a plagiarism checker cannot see. Only reading the abstract
      catches it. It is also the one an examiner is most likely to notice.

      **Reinhardt & Osei (2021) — fabricated.**
      There is no such article. The author names are invented, the DOI does not
      resolve, and no search of the journal's contents for volume 42 returns it.
      The citation is plausible in every superficial respect: a real journal, a
      volume number consistent with the year, a page range of a believable
      length, and a title that sounds like the literature.

      → The lesson: plausibility is manufactured. The only test is whether you
      can retrieve the item. Search the *title* in quotation marks, then the DOI.
      If neither returns anything, it does not exist, however confident the
      assistant was.

      ## Debrief questions

      - Which of the three took you longest, and why?
      - Which one would have survived into a submitted term paper?
      - Which capability class (Lecture 02, section 2) would have avoided each
        of these three failures — and which would not have helped at all?
      - How would you document this checking step in your AI disclosure?

      ========================================================================== --->

## Why this exercise exists

A fabricated reference is the easiest of the three problems to catch and the
least interesting. The dangerous case is the middle one: a real source, cited in
good faith, saying something other than what your sentence claims. No tool
catches that. Reading the abstract does.

This is the concrete meaning of the rule from the lecture: **never cite what you
have not read**, and *a citation you have not opened is not a citation*.

For how to record the checking you did, see
[Documenting and disclosing the use of AI](../ai-disclosure/index.qmd).
